modules.title: How Markets Work

objectives.text: Explain what an exchange, broker, clearing house and registry each do
Read a bid/ask quote and calculate spread cost
Distinguish market, limit and stop orders and when each can fail
Describe settlement cycles and why they matter

lessons.title: Who is in the market
lessons.body: A trade passes through several parties. The investor sends an order to a broker. The broker routes it to an exchange (e.g. ASX, LSE, NYSE, SGX) or another trading venue, where it is matched against an opposite order. After the match, a clearing house (central counterparty) stands between buyer and seller so neither carries the other's default risk. Settlement then moves cash and securities; a registry or depository records the new owner. Market makers and other liquidity providers post buy and sell quotes continuously and earn the spread in exchange for carrying inventory risk. Regulators (ASIC in Australia, the SEC in the US, the FCA in the UK, MAS in Singapore) set conduct and disclosure rules. Knowing the chain tells you where costs, delays and failures can appear.

lessons.title: Quotes, spread and depth
lessons.body: Every quote has a bid (highest price a buyer will pay) and an ask or offer (lowest price a seller will accept). The difference is the spread. Worked example (fictional): ABC Ltd quotes bid A$10.00, ask A$10.04. Spread = A$0.04. Mid-price = (10.00+10.04)/2 = A$10.02. Buying 1,000 shares at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses 1,000 x 0.04 = A$40 before brokerage; that is a round-trip spread cost of 0.04/10.02 = about 0.40%. Depth is how many shares sit at each price level. A tight spread with thin depth can still be expensive for a large order, because the order 'walks the book' to worse prices.

lessons.title: Order types
lessons.body: A market order executes immediately at the best available prices; it guarantees execution (in a normal market) but not price. A limit order sets the worst price you accept; it guarantees price but not execution. A stop (stop-loss) order becomes a market order once a trigger price trades; in a fast fall or an overnight gap it can fill well below the trigger. A stop-limit becomes a limit order at the trigger and may not fill at all. Time-in-force settings (day, good-till-cancelled, immediate-or-cancel) control how long an order lives. Example (fictional): you place a stop at A$9.50 on XYZ; the stock closes at A$9.80 and opens at A$9.10 after bad news. The stop triggers at the open and fills near A$9.10, not A$9.50.

lessons.title: Sessions, auctions and settlement
lessons.body: Many exchanges open and close with an auction, where orders accumulate and a single price is struck that maximises matched volume. Continuous trading happens between auctions. Trading halts and price limits pause markets on news or extreme moves. Settlement cycles differ by market and change over time (e.g. many equity markets have moved from T+2 toward T+1); always check the current rule for the venue. Settlement matters because unsettled funds may not be withdrawable, and selling shares you do not yet own creates fail risk. In the Transparent Trading app all trades are paper simulations: no real order reaches any venue.

lessons.title: Venues, fragmentation and fees
lessons.body: Shares may trade on several venues, including alternative venues and dark pools that do not display orders. Best-execution rules require brokers to seek good outcomes, but your actual cost is: spread + brokerage + any exchange/clearing fees + market impact. Example (fictional): buy A$5,000 of shares, brokerage A$9.50 each way, spread 0.20% round trip. Total round-trip cost = 9.50x2 + 0.002x5,000 = 19 + 10 = A$29, or 0.58% of the position. A trade must earn more than this just to break even.

modules.title: Shares, ETFs and Indices

objectives.text: Explain what a share represents and the rights attached
Compare ETFs, managed funds and individual shares
Understand how cap-weighted and equal-weighted indices are built
Calculate index weights and the effect of a constituent move

lessons.title: What a share is
lessons.body: A share (stock, equity) is a fractional ownership claim on a company's residual value after creditors. Ordinary shareholders typically get voting rights and any dividends declared, and rank last in liquidation. Preference shares usually have a fixed dividend and rank above ordinary shares. Corporate actions change share counts without changing company value: a 2-for-1 split doubles shares and halves price; a rights issue offers new shares, often at a discount, diluting those who do not take up. Example (fictional): you own 300 shares at A$12. A 3-for-1 split gives 900 shares at about A$4. Value stays A$3,600 before market moves.

lessons.title: ETFs and funds
lessons.body: An exchange-traded fund holds a basket (an index, sector, bonds, commodities) and trades on an exchange like a share. Key checks: management expense ratio (MER), tracking difference against its index, spread, size, replication method (physical full, sampled, or synthetic via swaps), and domicile (which affects withholding tax). Example: a fund with 0.20% MER on A$10,000 costs about A$20 per year in fees, deducted inside the fund price. Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily, so over several days their return can differ sharply from a simple multiple of the index.

lessons.title: How indices are built
lessons.body: An index is a rule-based basket used as a benchmark. Most major indices (S&P/ASX 200, S&P 500, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225 is an exception) are free-float market-cap weighted: weight = constituent float-adjusted market cap / total. The Nikkei 225 and Dow Jones Industrial Average are price-weighted, so high-priced shares dominate. Equal-weighted versions give each member the same weight at rebalance. Total-return indices reinvest dividends; price indices do not, so long-run comparisons must use the same type.

lessons.title: Index weight arithmetic
lessons.body: Worked example (fictional 3-stock index): A cap A$60bn, B A$30bn, C A$10bn; total A$100bn. Weights 60%, 30%, 10%. If A rises 5% and others are flat, index change = 0.60 x 5% = 3.0%. If C rises 20% and others flat, index change = 0.10 x 20% = 2.0%. Concentration therefore means a few large members drive most index moves; that is a risk to understand, not a flaw to ignore.

lessons.title: Global listings and share classes
lessons.body: Companies may list in several places (dual listings), issue depositary receipts (ADRs/GDRs), or have multiple share classes with different votes. Prices in different currencies must be FX-converted before comparing. Trading hours differ: Tokyo, Sydney, Hong Kong, London and New York sessions overlap only partially, so news may hit one listing first.

modules.title: Returns, Compounding and Honest P&L

objectives.text: Calculate simple, total and annualised returns
Separate realised from unrealised P&L and include all costs
Understand why drawdowns need larger gains to recover
Report performance honestly with cashflows considered

lessons.title: Simple and total return
lessons.body: Simple price return = (end price - start price)/start price. Total return adds income: (end - start + dividends)/start. Example (fictional): buy at A$50, receive A$2 dividend, sell at A$54. Price return = 4/50 = 8%. Total return = (4+2)/50 = 12%. Costs reduce both; with A$0.50 per share of round-trip costs, net total = 5.5/50 = 11%.

lessons.title: Compounding and annualising
lessons.body: Returns compound multiplicatively. Two years of +10% gives 1.1 x 1.1 - 1 = 21%, not 20%. Annualised (CAGR) = (end/start)^(1/years) - 1. Example: A$10,000 grows to A$14,641 in 4 years: (1.4641)^(0.25) - 1 = 10.0% per year. Never annualise a few days of results; a 2% week does not mean a sustainable 180% year.

lessons.title: Drawdowns and recovery
lessons.body: Drawdown = fall from a peak. Recovery needs gain = 1/(1-loss) - 1. A 20% loss needs 25% to recover; 50% needs 100%; 80% needs 400%. Max drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall over a period. It tells you what holding the strategy would have felt like, which average returns hide.

lessons.title: Realised, unrealised and fees
lessons.body: Realised P&L is locked in by closing; unrealised (mark-to-market) changes with price. Honest P&L includes brokerage, spreads, financing, FX conversion and borrow fees. Example: paper account A$100,000; realised +A$1,200, unrealised -A$900, costs A$150. Net change = 1,200 - 900 - 150 = A$150, i.e. +0.15%. Showing only the +A$1,200 would be misleading.

lessons.title: Cashflows and time-weighted returns
lessons.body: Deposits and withdrawals distort simple account growth. If an account goes A$10,000 to A$15,000 because you deposited A$5,000, return is 0%, not 50%. Time-weighted return (TWR) chains sub-period returns between cashflows and measures the strategy; money-weighted return (IRR) reflects your timing of deposits. Example: period 1 A$10,000 to A$11,000 (+10%); deposit A$5,000 so A$16,000; period 2 to A$15,200 (-5%). TWR = 1.10 x 0.95 - 1 = 4.5%.

modules.title: Interest Rates, Central Banks and Bonds

objectives.text: Explain how central banks set policy rates and transmit them
Price a simple bond and relate price to yield
Use duration to estimate price sensitivity
Read a yield curve and credit spreads
Interpret credit spreads and expected credit loss

lessons.title: Policy rates
lessons.body: Central banks such as the Reserve Bank of Australia (cash rate), US Federal Reserve (fed funds target range), European Central Bank, Bank of England and Bank of Japan set a short-term policy rate to pursue mandates such as price stability and employment. They implement it through open-market operations, standing facilities and interest on reserves, and may use balance-sheet tools (quantitative easing/tightening). Higher policy rates usually raise borrowing costs, slow credit growth and can strengthen the currency, though the effect is lagged and uncertain.

lessons.title: Bond basics and pricing
lessons.body: A bond pays coupons and returns face value at maturity. Price = present value of cashflows at the market yield. Example (fictional): 2-year A$100 face, 5% annual coupon, market yield 4%. Price = 5/1.04 + 105/1.04^2 = 4.808 + 97.078 = A$101.89. Because yield (4%) is below coupon (5%), the bond trades above par. Price and yield move inversely.

lessons.title: Duration and convexity
lessons.body: Modified duration estimates % price change for a 1-percentage-point yield change: dP/P ~ -Dmod x dy. Example: Dmod = 6, yields rise 0.50% gives about -3% price change. Longer maturity and lower coupon mean higher duration. Convexity makes the estimate less precise for large moves; for ordinary bonds actual price falls less and rises more than duration alone predicts.

lessons.title: Yield curve
lessons.body: The yield curve plots government yields against maturity. Normally upward sloping; an inverted curve (short yields above long) has historically preceded some recessions, but it is not a reliable timing tool. Steepening/flattening describes changes in the gap, e.g. 10-year minus 2-year spread. Real yields = nominal minus expected inflation; inflation-linked bonds show market-implied real yields.

lessons.title: Credit and spreads
lessons.body: Corporate bonds yield more than government bonds of similar maturity; the difference is the credit spread, compensating for default risk and lower liquidity. Ratings agencies grade issuers (investment grade vs high yield). Expected loss ~ probability of default x loss given default. Example: 2% annual PD and 60% LGD gives about 1.2% expected annual loss, so a spread of 1.0% would not cover it.

lessons.title: Pairs and quotes
lessons.body: FX is quoted as base/quote. AUD/USD = 0.6500 means 1 AUD buys 0.65 USD. If AUD/USD rises, AUD strengthened. Inverse: USD/AUD = 1/0.65 = 1.5385. Crosses like EUR/AUD can be derived: EUR/USD 1.08 / AUD/USD 0.65 = EUR/AUD 1.6615. The global FX market is the largest by turnover; the BIS Triennial Survey publishes turnover statistics.

lessons.title: Pips and P&L
lessons.body: For most pairs a pip is 0.0001 (for JPY pairs 0.01). Example (fictional paper trade): buy 100,000 AUD/USD at 0.6500, sell at 0.6550 = 50 pips. P&L = 100,000 x 0.0050 = US$500, converted to A$ at 0.6550: about A$763. Spreads in FX are quoted in pips; a 1.2-pip spread on 100,000 units costs US$12.

lessons.title: What moves currencies
lessons.body: Drivers include interest-rate differentials and expectations, inflation, trade and current account balances, commodity prices (AUD and CAD are linked to commodities), risk appetite (safe havens such as JPY, CHF, USD often rise in stress), capital flows and intervention. Forward FX prices reflect interest differentials (covered interest parity): forward = spot x (1+i_quote)/(1+i_base). This is not a forecast of future spot.

lessons.title: Currency in foreign investing
lessons.body: An Australian buying US shares has two returns: the share in USD and USD/AUD. Return in A$ = (1+r_asset)(1+r_fx) - 1. Example: US share +10%, USD falls 5% vs AUD: 1.10 x 0.95 - 1 = 4.5% in A$. Hedged funds remove most currency effect at a cost or benefit tied to rate differentials.

lessons.title: Leverage and carry in FX
lessons.body: Retail FX is often traded with margin; small moves produce large P&L. Carry trade: borrow low-yield currency, hold high-yield one; earns the differential but suffers sharp losses when risk appetite collapses. Many regulators (e.g. ASIC, ESMA) restrict retail leverage on CFDs and require negative-balance protection. This app is paper-only.

lessons.title: Commodity groups
lessons.body: Energy (crude oil benchmarks such as Brent and WTI, natural gas, LNG, coal), industrial metals (copper, aluminium, nickel, iron ore), precious metals (gold, silver) and agriculture (wheat, soybeans, sugar, coffee) each respond to different supply and demand forces: OPEC+ policy and inventories for oil; Chinese construction and steel output for iron ore; weather and planting for grains; real rates and central-bank buying for gold.

lessons.title: Futures curves
lessons.body: Most commodity exposure is via futures. Contango: later contracts priced above near ones (often when inventories are ample and storage costs apply). Backwardation: near contracts above later ones (tight supply). Example (fictional): front oil future A$100, next month A$102. A fund rolling monthly sells at 100 and buys at 102, roughly a 2% negative roll that month if prices stay unchanged.

lessons.title: Roll yield and fund returns
lessons.body: Commodity fund return ~ spot change + roll yield + collateral interest - fees. Example: spot flat over a year, roll -1% per month (~-11.4% compounded: 0.99^12-1), collateral 4%, fee 0.5%. Approximate return = -11.4% + 4% - 0.5% = about -7.9%. This is why a commodity ETF can fall even when spot prices end flat.

lessons.title: Producers and currencies
lessons.body: Miners and energy producers have operating leverage to prices: with costs of A$70 per unit and price A$100, margin is A$30; a 10% price rise to A$110 lifts margin 33% to A$40. Commodity exporters' currencies (AUD, CAD, NOK, BRL) often co-move with key exports. Physical delivery: futures can require delivery at expiry; retail paper practice should close or roll before expiry.

lessons.title: Data you can study for free
lessons.body: Government and agency sources publish inventories and outlooks (e.g. the US EIA weekly petroleum status report, Australia's Department of Industry Resources and Energy Quarterly, USDA WASDE). Exchanges publish contract specifications. Use these rather than paid feeds for study.

objectives.text: Describe how blockchains, consensus and stablecoins work
Identify custody and counterparty risk
Size positions for crypto volatility

lessons.title: What crypto-assets are
lessons.body: A blockchain is a shared ledger maintained by a network that validates transactions (proof-of-work or proof-of-stake). Bitcoin is a fixed-supply-schedule asset; Ether powers smart contracts on Ethereum. Stablecoins aim to track a currency via reserves or algorithms and have failed when reserves or designs proved weak. Crypto trades 24/7 across many venues worldwide, so prices can differ by venue.

lessons.title: Custody and counterparty risk
lessons.body: Self-custody means you hold private keys; losing them loses the assets. Exchange custody means you rely on the exchange's solvency and controls; exchange failures have caused large customer losses. Regulators such as ASIC (Moneysmart) warn that crypto-assets are high risk and many products are not covered by the protections that apply to traditional regulated investments.

lessons.title: Volatility and sizing
lessons.body: Crypto volatility is typically several times that of broad equity indices. Example: if annualised volatility is 70%, a rough one-day 1-standard-deviation move is 70%/sqrt(365) = about 3.7%. A A$5,000 paper position could swing about A$183 on an ordinary day and much more in stress. Size accordingly.

lessons.title: Perpetual futures and funding
lessons.body: Perpetual swaps have no expiry; a funding rate paid between longs and shorts keeps price near spot. Example: funding +0.01% every 8 hours on A$10,000 long = A$1 per period, A$3 per day, about A$1,095 per year (10.95%) if unchanged. High leverage on perpetuals leads to liquidation on small moves: at 20x, a ~5% adverse move wipes margin.

lessons.title: Scams and red flags
lessons.body: Guaranteed returns, pressure to move quickly, requests to send crypto to 'unlock' withdrawals, fake celebrity endorsements, and unsolicited 'account managers' are classic scam signs. Smart contracts can contain bugs; 'rug pulls' drain liquidity. Verify official sources; never share seed phrases.

lessons.title: Futures and forwards
lessons.body: A future is a standardised exchange-traded agreement to buy/sell at a set price later, margined daily (mark-to-market). A forward is a private, customised version. Example (fictional): an index future multiplier A$25 per point, index 7,800: notional = A$195,000. Initial margin 6% = A$11,700. A 1% fall (78 points) loses A$1,950, about 17% of margin.

lessons.title: Options payoffs
lessons.body: A call gives the right to buy at the strike; a put the right to sell. Buyer pays a premium; maximum loss = premium. Example: buy a A$50 call for A$2. At expiry: share A$56 profit = 56-50-2 = A$4; share A$51 = -A$1; below A$50 = -A$2. Breakeven = strike + premium = A$52. Put breakeven = strike - premium. Writing (selling) naked calls has theoretically unlimited loss.

lessons.title: Greeks
lessons.body: Delta: option price change per A$1 underlying move (call 0 to 1, put -1 to 0). Gamma: change of delta. Theta: time decay, usually negative for buyers. Vega: sensitivity to implied volatility. Example: call delta 0.40, share +A$1.00 gives option ~ +A$0.40.

lessons.title: CFDs and margin
lessons.body: A contract for difference pays the price change on an underlying without ownership, financed overnight. Leverage = notional / margin. At 20:1, a 5% adverse move loses 100% of margin. ASIC's product intervention order limits retail CFD leverage (e.g. 30:1 major FX, 2:1 crypto) and requires negative-balance protection; check current rules.

lessons.title: Swaps and hedging
lessons.body: Interest-rate swaps exchange fixed for floating payments; total-return swaps pass an asset's return. Hedging reduces risk but costs carry or premium: e.g. buying a put for 3% of portfolio value per year caps downside below the strike but drags returns if markets rise.

objectives.text: Measure liquidity using spread, volume and depth

lessons.title: Liquidity measures
lessons.body: Liquidity is ability to trade size quickly near the current price. Measures: spread (bps), average daily volume (ADV), depth at top levels, and turnover. Rule of thumb: keep orders a small fraction of ADV; trading 10% of ADV in one go often moves price noticeably. Small caps, frontier markets, and off-hours crypto are often thin.

lessons.title: Slippage and impact
lessons.body: Slippage = fill price minus decision (or arrival) price. Example: decide to buy at mid A$5.00, fill average A$5.03 on 10,000 shares: slippage = A$300 (0.6%). A common rough impact model: cost ~ k x volatility x sqrt(order size / ADV). It is an approximation, useful for comparing sizes, not exact prediction.

lessons.title: Financing, borrow and FX costs
lessons.body: Leveraged longs pay financing (e.g. benchmark + 3% annual on notional). Shorts pay borrow fees, which can spike for hard-to-borrow stocks, and must pay dividends to the lender. Example: A$20,000 short, borrow 2% annual for 30 days = 20,000 x 0.02 x 30/365 = A$32.88. Converting A$ to USD at a 0.5% FX margin costs A$50 per A$10,000 each way.

lessons.title: Tax caveats
lessons.body: Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction and personal circumstances: capital gains rules, holding period discounts (e.g. Australian CGT discount for some individuals holding over 12 months), franking credits, withholding tax on foreign dividends, and trader vs investor classification. This course gives general information only; check official sources such as the ATO, HMRC or IRS, or a qualified adviser. Paper trades have no tax effect.

lessons.title: Execution choices
lessons.body: Limit orders control price; splitting orders (TWAP/VWAP style) reduces impact; avoid illiquid open/close minutes unless using auctions deliberately; check news calendars. Measure your paper fills against arrival price so improvements are evidence-based.

objectives.text: Read the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement
Link the three statements
Calculate margins, leverage and liquidity ratios
Spot earnings-quality warning signs

lessons.title: Income statement
lessons.body: Revenue - cost of goods sold = gross profit; less operating expenses = operating profit (EBIT); less interest and tax = net profit. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortisation but ignores capital spending needs. Example (fictional, A$m): revenue 500, COGS 300, opex 120, D&A 20 included in opex, interest 10, tax 21. Gross 200 (40%), EBIT 80 (16%), EBITDA 100, pre-tax 70, net 49 (9.8%).

lessons.title: Balance sheet
lessons.body: Assets = liabilities + equity. Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) vs current liabilities (payables, short debt) gives the current ratio. Net debt = borrowings - cash. Example: current assets 150, current liabilities 100: current ratio 1.5. Debt 200, cash 50, EBITDA 100: net debt/EBITDA 1.5x.

lessons.title: Cash flow statement
lessons.body: Operating cash flow (OCF), investing (capex, acquisitions), financing (debt, dividends, buybacks). Free cash flow (FCF) ~ OCF - capex. Profit and cash differ due to working capital and non-cash items. Example: net profit 49, D&A +20, receivables up 15 (cash tied up): OCF ~ 54. Capex 30: FCF 24.

lessons.title: Linking statements
lessons.body: Net profit flows to retained earnings in equity; depreciation reduces asset values and is added back in OCF; capex adds to assets; debt raised appears in financing and liabilities. If profit consistently far exceeds OCF, investigate.

lessons.title: Quality red flags and standards
lessons.body: Warning signs: receivables growing much faster than revenue, frequent 'one-off' adjustments, capitalising ordinary costs, rising inventory days, auditor changes, related-party deals. Most listed companies outside the US report under IFRS (Australia uses AASB, aligned with IFRS); US companies use US GAAP and file 10-K reports. Read notes, not just headlines.

objectives.text: Calculate P/E, EV and EV/EBITDA

lessons.title: Multiples
lessons.body: P/E = price / earnings per share. Enterprise value (EV) = market cap + net debt (+ minorities, preferred). EV/EBITDA compares businesses with different debt. P/B = price / book value per share, useful for banks and insurers. Example (fictional): price A$20, EPS A$1.60: P/E 12.5. Market cap A$2bn, net debt A$0.5bn, EBITDA A$0.25bn: EV/EBITDA 10x.

lessons.title: Yields
lessons.body: Earnings yield = EPS/price (inverse of P/E). Dividend yield = DPS/price; in Australia franking credits may raise the grossed-up yield for eligible residents: grossed-up = cash yield / (1 - 0.30) for fully franked at a 30% company rate. Example: 4.2% fully franked = 6.0% grossed up. FCF yield = FCF / market cap.

lessons.title: Discounted cash flow
lessons.body: Value = sum of future FCF discounted at a required rate + terminal value. Gordon terminal value = FCF_next / (r - g). Example: FCF next year A$10m, r = 9%, g = 3%: TV = 10/0.06 = A$166.7m. Sensitivity: at r = 8%, 10/0.05 = A$200m. Small assumption changes move value a lot, so use ranges.

lessons.title: Unit metrics
lessons.body: Subscription: ARPU (average revenue per user), churn, CAC (customer acquisition cost), LTV ~ ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn. Example: ARPU A$30/month, margin 70%, churn 2%/month: LTV = 30 x 0.7 / 0.02 = A$1,050; CAC A$350 gives LTV/CAC 3.0. Retail: same-store sales, sales per square metre. Mining/energy: all-in sustaining cost (AISC) per ounce, cost per barrel. Airlines: RASK/CASK. Banks: net interest margin. Insurers: combined ratio.

lessons.title: Valuation traps
lessons.body: Cheap can be cheap for a reason: peak-cycle earnings make cyclicals look cheap at the top; one-off gains inflate EPS; heavy dilution erodes per-share value; high yields may precede dividend cuts. Compare to history and peers, and check cash conversion.

objectives.text: Analyse bank profitability via NIM, cost-to-income and loan losses

lessons.title: Bank economics
lessons.body: Banks earn net interest income (loan yield minus funding cost). NIM = net interest income / average interest-earning assets. Example (fictional): NII A$18bn, average earning assets A$900bn: NIM 2.0%. Cost-to-income = operating costs / operating income; lower is more efficient. Impairment charges rise in downturns; loan loss rate = impairments / gross loans.

lessons.title: Capital and funding
lessons.body: Basel III frameworks require minimum capital such as CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 / risk-weighted assets; national regulators (APRA in Australia) set specific requirements. Funding mix (deposits vs wholesale) and liquidity metrics (LCR, NSFR) matter: rapid deposit flight has toppled banks. ROE = net profit / equity; high ROE from thin capital is riskier.

lessons.title: Credit cycle
lessons.body: Credit growth, lending standards, house prices and unemployment drive bank earnings. Rising rates can widen NIM initially but raise defaults later. Watch arrears data and regulator stress tests.

lessons.title: Insurance
lessons.body: Combined ratio = (claims + expenses) / net earned premium. Example: claims A$650m, expenses A$280m, premiums A$1,000m: 93%, an underwriting profit. Insurers also earn on investment float. Catastrophe events, reserve strengthening and reinsurance costs are key risks. Life insurers are sensitive to interest rates and longevity.

lessons.title: Market infrastructure and asset managers
lessons.body: Exchanges and clearing houses earn per-trade, listing, data and clearing fees; revenues rise with volatility and volume. Payment networks earn per-transaction fees scaled with nominal spending. Asset managers earn fees on assets under management (AUM): revenue ~ AUM x fee rate, so market falls and outflows both hurt. Example: AUM A$100bn at 0.40% = A$400m revenue; a 15% market fall cuts it to A$340m before flows.

Example: crude A$110/bbl, products A$135/bbl: crack ~ A$25/bbl. Metrics: production (boe/d), reserves (1P/2P), reserve life = reserves / annual production, breakeven price.

lessons.body: Revenue ~ volume x price; cost metrics C1, AISC; grade (g/t gold, % copper) drives economics. Reserves vs resources differ in confidence (JORC Code in Australia, NI 43-101 in Canada). Example: AISC A$2,300/oz, gold A$3,000/oz: margin A$700/oz; 400koz produced = A$280m all-in margin. Risks: sovereign, permitting, tailings, cost inflation.

lessons.body: Many networks are regulated: allowed revenue ~ regulated asset base (RAB) x allowed return + depreciation + opex. Example: RAB A$10bn, allowed return 6%: return component A$600m. Example: RASK 12.0c, CASK 11.2c: unit margin 0.8c per available seat-km; a 5% fuel cost rise can wipe this out.

lessons.title: Consumer staples vs discretionary

Discretionary (retail, autos, travel, restaurants) is cyclical; analyse same-store (like-for-like) sales, inventory turnover, and consumer confidence. Example: revenue +6% = price +8%, volume -2%: growth driven by price, which may not last.

lessons.title: Health care
lessons.body: Pharma/biotech: pipelines by phase (Phase I-III success rates are low), patent cliffs, regulator approvals (TGA, FDA, EMA). Devices and services: procedure volumes, reimbursement rates. lessons.title: Real estate and REITs
lessons.body: REITs own property and distribute most income. Metrics: net tangible assets (NTA) per security, funds from operations (FFO), gearing = net debt / total assets, occupancy, weighted average lease expiry (WALE), cap rate = net operating income / property value. Example: NOI A$50m, value A$1bn: cap rate 5%. If cap rates rise to 5.5%, value = 50/0.055 = A$909m (-9.1%).

lessons.title: Sector rotation
lessons.body: Defensives (staples, utilities, health) often outperform in slowdowns; cyclicals (industrials, discretionary, materials) in recoveries. This is a tendency, not a rule; GICS from MSCI and S&P provides standard sector classification.

modules.title: Macro, News and Catalysts

objectives.text: Read key macro releases
Explain surprise vs expectations pricing
Map company and index catalysts
Assess news quality using primary sources
Run a calendar-driven event-risk process

lessons.title: Macro releases
lessons.body: Inflation (CPI, trimmed mean, core PCE), labour (unemployment, payrolls, wages), activity (GDP, retail sales, PMIs where above 50 indicates expansion), and trade data. National statistics agencies (e.g. ABS, US BLS, Eurostat, ONS) publish schedules in advance. Central bank meetings and minutes drive rate expectations.

lessons.title: Surprise matters
lessons.body: Markets price expectations. Example: consensus CPI 3.0%, actual 3.4% = +0.4pp surprise; bond yields may jump even though inflation 'only' rose slightly. A strong result already expected can lead to a fall ('buy the rumour, sell the fact'). Compare to consensus and to what is priced (e.g. rate futures implied probabilities).

lessons.title: Company catalysts
lessons.body: Earnings and guidance changes, dividends, buybacks, M&A, capital raisings, index inclusion/exclusion, regulatory decisions, trial results, and lock-up expiries. Continuous disclosure rules (ASX Listing Rule 3.1) require prompt release of price-sensitive information; trading on inside information is illegal.

lessons.title: News quality
lessons.body: Distinguish primary sources (company announcements, central bank statements, official statistics) from commentary and social media. Check timestamps, avoid trading headlines you cannot verify, beware AI-generated or fake news. Ask: is this new, material, and not already priced?

lessons.title: Event risk process
lessons.body: Keep a weekly calendar; reduce size or avoid opening new positions just before binary events unless the event is the planned thesis; pre-define what result invalidates the trade. Example rule: halve paper position size if a scheduled event's implied move exceeds 2x normal daily range.

modules.title: Technical Analysis: Trend, Mean Reversion and Volatility

objectives.text: Use moving averages and breakouts to define trend
Use z-scores and oscillators for mean reversion
Measure volatility with ATR and standard deviation
Test technical rules honestly rather than trusting chart patterns

lessons.title: Trend tools
lessons.body: Simple moving average (SMA) = average of last N closes. A common trend filter: price above 200-day SMA. Breakout: price exceeds N-day high. Trend rules tend to have low win rates but larger winners; they suffer in choppy markets.

lessons.title: Mean reversion
lessons.body: Z-score = (price - mean)/standard deviation over a lookback. Example: 20-day mean A$50, sd A$2, price A$46: z = -2.0. RSI measures recent gains vs losses (0-100; <30 'oversold'). Mean reversion tends to work better in range-bound markets and fails when a new trend begins.

lessons.title: Volatility
lessons.body: Average true range (ATR) = average of max(high-low, |high-prev close|, |low-prev close|). Annualised volatility ~ daily sd x sqrt(252) for exchange-traded assets. Example: daily sd 1.2%: about 19% annual. Volatility clusters: calm and turbulent periods persist. Implied volatility (from options, e.g. VIX for S&P 500) reflects expected volatility.

lessons.title: Support, resistance and patterns
lessons.body: Support and resistance are zones where buying/selling previously appeared. Patterns (head-and-shoulders, flags) are subjective; different people draw different lines. Convert any idea into an exact rule before testing.

lessons.title: Testing rules
lessons.body: Write the rule exactly (entry, exit, sizing, costs). Test across markets and periods, include costs, count trades, and compare to buy-and-hold. Without testing, chart reading is storytelling. Module 20 covers bias.

modules.title: Position Sizing, Correlation, Stops and Gaps

objectives.text: Size positions by fixed fractional risk
Adapt size to volatility (ATR)
Use correlation to understand concentration
Design stops with realistic gap risk
Apply drawdown limits, heat caps and kill switches

lessons.title: Fixed fractional sizing
lessons.body: Risk per trade = account x risk %. Shares = risk / (entry - stop). Example (fictional): A$100,000 paper account, 0.5% risk = A$500; entry A$25.00, stop A$23.75 (A$1.25): 400 shares = A$10,000 position. Many professionals keep per-trade risk to a small fraction of capital.

lessons.title: Volatility sizing
lessons.body: Set stop distance in ATR multiples (e.g. 2 x ATR) so size adapts: if ATR A$0.80, stop distance A$1.60; at A$500 risk, 312 shares. Higher volatility, smaller size.

lessons.title: Correlation
lessons.body: Correlation (-1 to +1) measures co-movement. Five 'different' bank shares with 0.8 correlation behave like one large position. Portfolio variance for two assets: w1^2 s1^2 + w2^2 s2^2 + 2 w1 w2 rho s1 s2. Example: 50/50, each 20% vol, rho 0.5: variance = 0.01+0.01+0.01 = 0.03; vol 17.3%. With rho 1.0: 20%. Correlations tend to rise in crises.

lessons.title: Stops and gaps
lessons.body: Stops limit typical losses but gaps skip them. Example: 400 shares, stop A$23.75, gap open A$21.00: loss = 400 x 4.00 = A$1,600, 3.2x planned risk. Stress test: assume worst plausible gap (e.g. 3x normal) for overnight and event positions. Options or smaller size can cap gap risk.

lessons.title: Drawdown limits
lessons.body: Pre-set rules: e.g. cut size by half after a 5% account drawdown; pause new trades after 10% and review. Firm-level heat cap: total open risk (sum of stop distances) e.g. <= 3% of equity. Rules must be written before trading.

modules.title: Performance Metrics and Statistical Confidence

objectives.text: Calculate win rate, payoff ratio, expectancy and R-multiples
Calculate Sharpe and Sortino ratios
Judge sample size and confidence
Report metrics honestly

lessons.title: R-multiples and expectancy
lessons.body: R = initial risk per trade. A trade risking A$500 that makes A$1,000 is +2R. Expectancy per trade = win rate x average win - loss rate x average loss. Example: 40% wins averaging 2.5R, 60% losses averaging 1R: E = 0.4x2.5 - 0.6x1 = +0.40R. Payoff ratio = avg win / avg loss = 2.5.

lessons.title: Win rate is not enough
lessons.body: A 90% win-rate strategy with average win 0.1R and average loss 1.5R: E = 0.09 - 0.15 = -0.06R, a loser. Profit factor = gross profit / gross loss.

lessons.title: Sharpe and Sortino
lessons.body: Sharpe = (return - risk-free) / standard deviation of returns. Example: 12% return, 4% risk-free, 16% vol: Sharpe 0.5. Sortino uses downside deviation: with downside deviation 10%, Sortino = 0.8. Annualise consistently; serial correlation and fat tails distort Sharpe.

lessons.title: Sample size and confidence
lessons.body: Standard error of mean R = sd(R)/sqrt(n). Example: mean 0.3R, sd 1.5R, n = 25: SE = 0.3; t = 1.0, weak evidence. n = 225: SE = 0.1, t = 3.0, stronger. Rough rule: fewer than ~30 trades says little; even hundreds can mislead if regimes change.

lessons.title: Honest reporting
lessons.body: Report: number of trades, period, net of costs, max drawdown, best/worst trades, exposure time, and paper vs live. Never report only winners, cherry-picked windows or gross returns. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

modules.title: Backtesting, Bias and Validation

objectives.text: Identify look-ahead, survivorship, selection and overfitting biases
Use holdout and walk-forward testing
Correct for multiple testing
Use cost stress and counterfactual benchmarks
Decide when a paper result is credible

lessons.title: Common biases
lessons.body: Look-ahead bias: using data not available at decision time (e.g. revised earnings, same-day close for a decision made at the open). Survivorship bias: testing only today's surviving index members ignores delisted losers. Selection/data-snooping: trying many rules and reporting the best. Overfitting: too many parameters for the data.

lessons.title: Holdout and walk-forward
lessons.body: Split data: develop on in-sample, then test once on untouched holdout. Walk-forward: optimise on window 1, test on next window, roll forward, and stitch out-of-sample results. Example: 10 years; train on 3, test next 1, roll yearly: 7 out-of-sample years.

lessons.title: Multiple testing
lessons.body: If you test 20 independent useless rules at 5% significance, expect about 1 'significant' by chance (20 x 0.05). Probability at least one appears significant = 1 - 0.95^20 = about 64%. Adjust thresholds (e.g. Bonferroni: 0.05/20 = 0.0025) or demand out-of-sample proof.

lessons.title: Costs and counterfactuals
lessons.body: Re-run with doubled costs and delayed fills; if the edge vanishes, it was fragile. Counterfactuals: compare to buy-and-hold, random entries with the same exits, and the same rule on other markets. Example: strategy +8% p.a., random-entry benchmark +7.5%: edge is mostly exposure, not timing.

lessons.title: Credibility checklist
lessons.body: Economic rationale; few parameters; stable across nearby settings; positive out-of-sample; survives cost stress; adequate trades; documented before forward paper test. Forward paper testing is the final check before any consideration of real capital, and even then outcomes are not guaranteed.

modules.title: Disciplined Paper Practice, Ethics and Critical Thinking with AI

objectives.text: Run a structured paper trading process with journals and reviews
Apply ethics: market integrity, honesty and conflicts
Use AI tools critically and verify outputs
Plan responsible next steps without promised profits

lessons.title: Process over outcomes
lessons.body: A trading plan lists: markets, setups, entry/exit rules, sizing, risk limits, review schedule. Journal every paper trade: thesis, evidence, plan, result, emotion, lesson. Review weekly: rule-following rate, expectancy, mistakes. Good decisions can lose; bad ones can win; judge the process across many trades.

lessons.title: Psychology and behaviour
lessons.body: Common biases: loss aversion, overconfidence, recency, confirmation bias, revenge trading, FOMO. Counter with checklists, pre-commitment, cooling-off rules (e.g. no new trades after 3 consecutive losses in a day).

lessons.title: Ethics and market integrity
lessons.body: Never spread false information, manipulate prices (pump-and-dump, spoofing, wash trading), or trade on inside information. Disclose conflicts when discussing investments. Professional codes such as the CFA Institute Code of Ethics emphasise integrity, diligence and putting clients first. Be honest about paper vs real results.

lessons.title: AI critically
lessons.body: AI assistants can summarise, calculate and generate ideas, but can be wrong, out of date, or fabricate sources. Verify facts with primary sources, check calculations, ask for assumptions, and never let an AI tool override your risk limits. AI signals in this app are paper-only educational tools, not advice.

lessons.title: Next steps responsibly
lessons.body: This course is general education, not personal financial advice and not a regulated qualification. Before real money: understand your goals, emergency fund, debts, tax and product disclosure documents; consider licensed advice. No strategy guarantees profits; losses can exceed expectations.
